cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-45-christ.summary: Within a great walled city, 'the city of God', the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos stands upright in a mandorla between groups of the faithful — 'God is in the midst of her' — while others sit in the streams of the river that makes the city glad. Angels blow trumpets in the sky, the voice at which the earth melts. The drawing pictures the psalm that inspired Luther's later hymn 'A mighty fortress'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-45-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-109-the-l.summary: To illustrate 'The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool', the artist placed Christ incarnate, cross-nimbed, on a throne beside the Christ-Logos seated on a globe, both within one mandorla among angels, with two enemies prostrate at Christ's feet. Below, the saints gather in the rays of the morning star and Christ's enemies are overthrown. The psalm is the most quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-109-the-l.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-widows-mite.summary: Seated beneath the arcades of the Temple with apostles behind him, Christ points to a poor widow who drops her two coins into the treasury box. The Index of Medieval Art catalogues this page as fol. 192r; the generous gesture of the small figure is the centre of the composition.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-widows-mite.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 387); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-sma-christ-enthroned-fath.summary: Along the left aisle, a long row of standing saints and Fathers of the Western and Eastern Churches converges on the enthroned Christ at the centre, while scenes from the Old Testament stories of Noah and Joseph run in a frieze above. The great wall gathers the whole Church, Latin and Greek, around Christ.
facts: Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum preserves wall paintings from the 6th to the late 8th century; buried after an earthquake in 847, it was rediscovered only in 1900.
Inscriptions in the church shift from Greek (under Martin I) to Greek and Latin (under John VII) and finally Latin alone (under Paul I), reflecting Rome's changing ties to Byzantium.

cur:monumental-sma-christ-enthroned-fath.notes: The photograph shows the whole wall; Christ is the central enthroned figure.

walters:71.277.summary: Beneath a pointed trefoil arch with a crocketed gable, Christ hangs from the cross crowned with thorns, his head fallen to one side. At the left, the swooning Virgin is held up by the other holy women; at the right stand John, holding a book with his hand on his breast, and a bearded man in a hat. Though coarsely carved and much rubbed, the large leaf conveys the grief of the Passion with clarity.
facts: The Walters describes the group at the left as the Three Marys and the bearded figure at the right as 'a Hebrew', standing beside John.
The leaf, almost 20 cm high, was once hinged to a companion panel; its hinges are lost.
It was in the collection of Raoul Heilbronner (sold in Paris, 1921) before Henry Walters bought it the same year.
walters:71.277.notes: The Walters date label reads '3rd quarter 14th century' but the date fields give 1375–1400; 'second half of the 14th century' covers both. Worklist year 800 was a parsing error.

feat:ushakov-saviour-not-made-by-hands.summary: The face of Christ, without a body, appears upon a white cloth held up as if by unseen hands, recalling the legend of the image Christ miraculously impressed on a towel for King Abgar of Edessa. Ushakov, a royal icon painter who later led the painters of the Kremlin Armoury, softened the traditional icon with gentle modelling and naturalistic shading. His version of this image became one of the most copied images of Christ in Russia.
facts: Ushakov and his circle painted the subject many times; this signed 1658 icon from the Trinity Church in Nikitniki, Moscow, is the earliest to survive.
In a treatise on painting, Ushakov defended a more lifelike style, comparing the icon painter to a mirror that faithfully reflects what it shows.
The legend of the Mandylion, the image 'not made by hands', underpinned Byzantine and Russian arguments that Christ himself authorised his own portrait.
